candidate.frame: We’re using a capacity lens, not a streak lens: are we steadier when the phone is off and real life intrudes? If the calm evaporates between sessions, you’ve already seen the dependency trap—now we pivot to skills that stick, not hits of relief.

Use any app only as scaffolding: practice off‑cue, in different locations and moods, and measure progress in reactivity and behavior, not consecutive days logged (per Linardon 2019).

candidate.hook: You stretch your hips, fire up your glutes, and still can’t hit depth—because the real limiter is your ankles, not your hips. Improve dorsiflexion a little, and your squat drops lower fast.
candidate.frame: We’ve all done the hip work; now we’re looking at depth through the balance-and-levers lens. A bit more ankle dorsiflexion lets your knees travel, keeps you over midfoot, and unlocks the bottom.
candidate.payload: Depth is governed by how far your knees can travel while keeping your center of mass over midfoot—i.e., ankle dorsiflexion—not by how “open” your hips feel (per Schoenfeld 2010). When dorsiflexion is restricted, lifters compensate with earlier hip hinge, more forward torso lean, and shallower knee/hip flexion; elevate the heel or increase dorsiflexion and depth improves immediately (per Sato 2012; Sinclair 2014). Greater weight‑bearing lunge test distances are associated with deeper squats and less trunk lean, indicating ankle mobility predicts depth better than isolated hip measures (per Rabin and Kozol 2017). Mechanistically, more dorsiflexion increases tibial inclination, shortens the hip‑to‑midfoot moment arm, and delays posterior pelvic tilt, letting you stay balanced while dropping lower (per Schoenfeld 2010). That’s why small dorsiflexion bumps from a heel wedge, lifting shoes, or targeted soleus work can unlock a noticeably deeper bottom even when hip stretching hasn’t helped (per Sinclair 2014). Screen with the weight‑bearing lunge test and train with calf eccentrics, long‑duration stretches, and ankle joint mobilizations, then retest depth under the same stance and load (per Rabin and Kozol 2017).
candidate.bridge: Squat depth is like trying to sit down in ski boots—lock the ankles and you can only fold at the waist; free them (or add a small heel) and you drop lower while staying balanced.

candidate.topic: Why ankle flexibility predicts squat depth more than hip mobility
candidate.hook: Hip mobility barely predicts how deep you squat—ankle dorsiflexion does. If your heels want to lift at the bottom, your ankles—not your hips—are the bottleneck.
candidate.frame: As lifters chasing clean depth, we read squats from the floor up. We’ll use ankle dorsiflexion as the primary constraint shaping knee travel and torso angle, then see where hip mobility actually fits.
candidate.payload: Start from the floor: without enough ankle dorsiflexion, the tibia can’t incline forward, so the knees can’t travel over the toes; to keep balance, you’re forced to push the hips back and lean the torso, which runs you out of hip flexion room sooner and stops depth early (per Escamilla 2001; Schoenfeld 2010). When dorsiflexion is artificially increased—via heel wedges or weightlifting shoes—lifters achieve more knee flexion and a more upright torso, typically hitting deeper positions with the same hips (per Sato 2012; Sinclair 2014). That’s why ankle dorsiflexion often predicts squat depth better than “hip mobility”: ankle range sets the forward-knee window that governs center-of-mass over midfoot and the pelvis’s clearance at the bottom (per Schoenfeld 2010). Hip mobility still matters for comfort and knee-out (abduction/external rotation) and can reduce impingement, but it rarely unlocks depth if the ankle is the bottleneck (per Escamilla 2001). If your heels want to pop, quantify closed-chain dorsiflexion with a weight‑bearing lunge test and address it directly—then reassess depth (per Bennell 1998).
candidate.bridge: Deep squatting is like parallel parking: if your front wheels (ankles) can’t turn far, you have to swing the back end (hips/torso) way out and still stop short. Give the wheels more angle with a heel wedge and you slide into a deeper spot with the same hips.
